items.topic: Basis for testing hedge effectiveness: changes in value, not levels
items.definition: A hedge is effective when a $1 move in the hedged item's price is matched by a roughly $1 offsetting move in the hedge's value. Because of this, effectiveness testing compares period-to-period changes in value between the hedge and the hedged item, not their absolute price levels.
items.core_idea: Hedge quality is judged by how closely the day-to-day value changes of the hedge track the day-to-day value changes of the hedged item, rather than by comparing the two items' price levels directly.
key_points: The ideal hedge offsets the hedged item's value change roughly dollar-for-dollar.
Effectiveness tests use day-to-day (or period-to-period) changes in value, not the values themselves.
This distinction matters because comparing raw price levels would not reveal whether the two positions move together.
relationships: Feeds into regression-based effectiveness tests (slope, R-squared) described in the same section.
trading_implications: When building a hedge test, prepare a changes-in-value (or percent-change) series for both instruments before running any statistical analysis.
common_misunderstandings: Assuming hedge effectiveness can be judged by comparing the two items' price levels rather than their changes in value.

items.topic: Adjusting hedge size for mismatched volatility
items.definition: When the hedge instrument is more or less volatile than the hedged item, the notional size of the hedge must be scaled to compensate so that the dollar changes in value line up, and a pre-processing step (computing changes or percent changes in value) is needed before regression analysis.
items.core_idea: If the hedge is, for example, twice as volatile as the hedged item, the hedge should be sized at roughly half the hedged item's size so their value changes stay comparable; mismatched volatility requires converting price series to value changes (or percent changes) before running a regression to test effectiveness.
key_points: A hedge twice as volatile as the hedged item should be sized at about half the hedged item's notional.
Prior to regression analysis, an extra step converts price series into changes in value, or percent changes in value, when volatilities are mismatched.
relationships: Precedes the regression-based statistical tests (slope, R-squared, etc.) covered later in the section.
trading_implications: Size a hedge relative to the ratio of volatilities between the hedge and the hedged item rather than assuming a 1:1 notional match.
common_misunderstandings: Assuming a 1:1 notional hedge is always correct regardless of the relative volatility of the two instruments.

items.topic: Five prospective regression tests for hedge effectiveness
items.definition: A regression of the hedge's value changes against the hedged item's value changes produces summary statistics; a commonly used framework applies five tests to that regression's output to decide whether a hedge qualifies as highly effective.
items.core_idea: After running linear regression on the value changes of the hedge and hedged item, practitioners commonly check five statistics — slope, R-squared, slope significance, F-test significance, and sample count — against threshold values to judge whether the hedge is highly effective.
key_points: Test 1 (Slope): the regression slope should fall between -0.80 and -1.25, meaning a $1.00 move in the hedged item should be offset by roughly $0.80 to $1.25 in the hedge.
Test 2 (R-squared): R2 measures how well the paired observations fit the regression line; a commonly used threshold requires R2 greater than 0.80.
Test 3 (Slope significance): checks whether the slope estimate is statistically meaningful, commonly by requiring the t-statistic's p-value to be below 0.05.
Test 4 (F-test significance): a secondary test analogous to Test 3 but for the R2 estimate, commonly by requiring the F-statistic's p-value to be below 0.05.
Test 5 (Number of samples): checks that enough observations were used for the test to be valid; commonly 30 or more samples.
A p-value is the probability output of a statistical test used to judge pass/fail against a threshold like 0.05.

Statistical significance compares an estimate to its error band: a small error relative to the estimate is significant (e.g., $1 million +/- $50,000), while a large error relative to the estimate is not (e.g., $1 million +/- $10 million).
In practice, spreadsheet or statistical software computes these values automatically; the user's role is to read and interpret the output against the thresholds.
relationships: Builds on the changes-in-value framing and volatility-adjusted sizing described earlier in this section.
trading_implications: A hedge failing the slope range, R2 threshold, or sample-size test would not be classified as highly effective under this framework, which matters for hedge accounting/documentation.
The slope's sign convention here is negative, reflecting that an effective hedge's value should move opposite to the hedged item's value.
common_misunderstandings: Treating R2 alone as sufficient without also checking slope range, significance tests, and sample size.
Confusing a small p-value requirement with the underlying idea of statistical significance (which compares estimate size to error-band size).
